questions.question: Which broad purpose takes the largest share of UK public spending?

options.B: Social protection, including state pensions and benefits

questions.why: HM Treasury PESA functional tables show social protection as the largest spending function, ahead of health.

questions.question: In recent years, total UK public spending has been closest to what share of national income (GDP)?
questions.why: Total managed expenditure has been roughly 40-46% of GDP in recent years according to OBR and HM Treasury figures.

questions.question: Why compare spending across decades in real terms or as a share of GDP, rather than in cash pounds?

options.B: Cash figures rise with inflation even if real spending is unchanged
options.D: There is no reason; they mean the same

questions.why: Inflation raises cash amounts over time, so cash comparisons overstate real growth.

questions.question: Which single tax raises the most money for the UK government?
questions.why: OBR and HMRC receipts show income tax as the largest single source of revenue.

questions.question: Which three taxes together raise the largest share of UK government receipts?

options.A: Council tax, stamp duty, fuel duty
options.B: Income tax, National Insurance contributions, VAT
options.C: Corporation tax, alcohol duty, tobacco duty
options.D: Inheritance tax, capital gains tax, air passenger duty

questions.why: Income tax, National Insurance and VAT are consistently the three biggest revenue sources.

questions.question: When government spending is higher than its receipts in a year, how is the gap mainly covered?
questions.why: Public sector net borrowing is the gap between spending and receipts; borrowing is not a tax.

questions.question: Which of these is a government receipt that is NOT a tax?

options.C: Interest and dividends received by government

questions.why: ONS public sector finances list interest and dividends as non-tax receipts, separate from taxes.

questions.question: Roughly what share of all income tax is paid by the top 1% of income taxpayers?

options.C: About a quarter to a third

questions.why: HMRC income tax liabilities statistics have shown the top 1% paying roughly 25-30% of income tax for over a decade.

questions.question: If the top 1% pay about 28% of income tax, what does the 28% describe?

options.B: Their share of total income tax collected
options.C: The share of their income paid in all taxes

questions.why: It is a share of total revenue, not a tax rate on anyone's income.

questions.question: According to ONS, which household group pays the most tax per household in pounds?

options.D: All fifths pay the same in pounds

questions.why: ONS Effects of taxes and benefits shows the richest fifth paying far more tax in cash per household.

questions.question: According to ONS, which group pays the largest share of its disposable income in indirect taxes such as VAT?

options.D: Every group pays exactly the same share

questions.why: ONS consistently finds indirect taxes take a larger share of disposable income for the poorest fifth.

questions.question: In ONS household tax statistics, which of these counts as an indirect tax?
questions.why: ONS treats VAT and duties as indirect taxes; income tax, employee NICs and council tax are direct.

questions.question: Across all UK households, roughly what share of gross income goes on direct and indirect taxes combined, according to ONS?
questions.why: ONS Effects of taxes and benefits has put all taxes at roughly a third of gross household income on average.

questions.question: An average household pays about 35% of gross income in all taxes. Does that mean people face a 35% income tax rate?

options.B: No, it is a household average combining direct and indirect taxes
options.D: No, it is the share of all tax revenue

questions.why: A household average of combined taxes is neither a personal tax rate nor a share of total revenue.

questions.question: Why can the poorest households' indirect taxes look very high relative to their income?

options.A: They pay a higher VAT rate
options.B: Some spend more than their measured income, so taxes on spending are large relative to income

questions.why: ONS notes low-income households may spend more than their income, raising indirect tax as a share of income.

questions.question: Since the 1970s, how has the mix of UK jobs changed?

options.B: Service jobs have grown as a share while manufacturing has shrunk

questions.why: ONS workforce jobs data show a long shift from manufacturing to services.

questions.question: Cash pay rose 50% over a period while prices rose 40%. What happened to pay after inflation?
questions.why: 1.50 divided by 1.40 is about 1.07, a real rise of roughly 7%.

questions.question: Between 2008 and 2014, what happened to average weekly pay in Great Britain after adjusting for inflation?
questions.why: ONS real average weekly earnings fell for several years after the 2008 financial crisis.

questions.question: In England today, which is the most common housing tenure?

options.C: Owner occupation, outright or with a mortgage

questions.why: The English Housing Survey shows about two thirds of households in England are owner occupiers.

questions.question: According to ONS travel statistics, which country do UK residents visit most often?
questions.why: ONS Travel Trends consistently shows Spain as the most visited country by UK residents.

questions.question: A travel survey was paused for most of 2020. How should a chart show that year?

options.A: Draw a straight line from 2019 to 2021
options.C: Show it as missing, with a note

questions.why: The International Passenger Survey was suspended in 2020; filling the gap would invent continuity.

questions.question: In England, infant classes (ages 5 to 7) are by law generally limited to how many pupils per school teacher?
questions.why: The School Admissions (Infant Class Sizes) regulations cap infant classes at 30 per teacher, with limited exceptions.

questions.question: Why should a class-size figure say which nation and school phase it covers?

options.A: Education is devolved and primary and secondary classes differ, so figures are not interchangeable
options.B: It is only a design choice
options.C: All UK nations publish one shared figure
options.D: Secondary classes are always bigger than primary

questions.why: Each UK nation collects its own school data, and class sizes differ by phase, so mixing them misleads.

questions.question: A site shows an 'example family' and the tax they pay. What is this?

options.B: The official average for all households
options.C: An illustration built on assumptions, not a measured figure

questions.why: An example family is a modelled illustration and should not be presented as measured fact.
